items.title: Rödl initialization upgrades generalized niceness to a restricted set, a complete or anticomplete blockade, or a polynomial clique or stable set
items.strategy: Apply Rödl at the fixed scale used by the preceding generalized-niceness page. If the requested parameter x is already above that scale, the Rödl subgraph gives the restricted outcome immediately. Otherwise run the published constant-scale generalized-niceness lemma on the Rödl subgraph and choose the final exponent large enough to absorb the linear-size loss when the outcome is transferred back to G.

items.title: Large induced subgraphs without a polynomial clique or stable set force complete or anticomplete blockades
items.strategy: Assume a large induced subgraph F admits no complete or anticomplete blockade of the target polynomial width. Apply the Rödl-initialized lemma to F. A restricted outcome gives a polynomial clique or stable set by the published restricted-set bound, the blockade outcome contradicts the hypothesis on F, and the remaining source outcome already is the desired polynomial clique or stable set.

items.title: Leaf-reducible wonderful generalized nice finite families have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Choose x and epsilon as in the source proof. The previous lemma makes every epsilon^(2c_1)-large induced subgraph satisfy the hypothesis of the published blockade-to-restricted theorem. The resulting epsilon-restricted induced subgraph is still large enough that the published restricted-set bound gives a clique or stable set of size |G|^c, contradicting the assumed failure of Erdős–Hajnal.

title: From Generalized Niceness to Erdős–Hajnal — Examples

items.title: The Lemma 3.5 parameter choice on a graph of order just above the source threshold
items.strategy: Take a sample value of c_1 and a graph order slightly above 2^(42c_1^2), compute x and epsilon exactly as in the source, and verify numerically that x < epsilon <= 1/4 and that the claimed lower bounds on |F| and |S| really exceed epsilon^(-1).

items.title: A complete four-blockade gives a four-vertex clique
items.strategy: Choose one vertex from each block of a complete four-blockade and check directly that the chosen vertices are pairwise adjacent, illustrating the blockade branch of Claim 3.5.1 without extra exponent bookkeeping.

items.title: A large epsilon-restricted induced subgraph gives a polynomial clique or stable set
items.strategy: Work through a concrete epsilon-restricted induced subgraph whose order exceeds epsilon^(-1), apply the published restricted-set bound, and compare the resulting clique or stable-set size with the final power of |G| used in the proof of Lemma 3.5.

items.title: Property (*) for a finite graph family
Property (*) and leaf reducibility yield five comb outcomes in a restricted graph
items.strategy: Handle the dense-side case by the published leaf-reducible lemma in the complement. Otherwise run the published sparse comb lemma. The first two sparse exits already give the large pair and deeper-restriction outcomes; on the comb exit, apply property (*) and translate its three branches into the clique-or-stable-set, complete-or-anticomplete blockade, and pure blockade outcomes.

items.title: Property (*) and leaf reducibility yield a long x-sparse or complete blockade, or a better outcome
items.strategy: Apply the previous five-outcome lemma inside each c|G|-large induced subgraph. If the large-pair outcome is always present, invoke the published maximal-blockade theorem to obtain a long x-sparse or complete blockade. Otherwise choose a large induced subgraph where that pair outcome fails and convert the surviving local exit into one of the remaining four global outcomes by direct exponent comparisons.

items.title: Under failure of the global outcomes, a large y^(10/3)-restricted induced subgraph forces a y^(11/3)-restricted induced subgraph
items.strategy: Assume a large y^(10/3)-restricted induced subgraph F has no y^(11/3)-restricted subgraph of the required relative size. Apply the previous lemma to F. The sparse-or-complete blockade, clique-or-stable-set, and complete-or-anticomplete blockade exits all convert directly into the forbidden global outcomes after exponent bookkeeping, so only the deeper restricted-set exit can survive.

items.title: Constant-scale restricted property (*) yields a restricted subgraph, a polynomial clique or stable set, or two blockade alternatives
items.strategy: Use the previous claim to verify the hypothesis of the published iterative restricted-sparsification lemma with the source exponents b_1 = 11/10, b_2 = 3(c_4+2), and b_3 = 3(c_4+2)/10. The iterative lemma gives the restricted-set outcome; the other three outcomes are the direct global exits that remain visible in the statement.

items.title: Rödl initialization removes the constant-scale restriction in the property (*) four-outcome theorem
items.strategy: Use Rödl at the fixed scale c^10 to obtain a linear-size restricted induced subgraph F. Apply the preceding constant-scale theorem to F and absorb the Rödl loss into a sufficiently large exponent d. In the pure-or-x-sparse blockade branch, replace l by a comparable integer k roughly equal to sqrt(l) so the blockade matches the page's polynomial-width normal form.

items.title: Large induced subgraphs in the property (*) four-outcome theorem contain a pure or x-sparse polynomial blockade
items.strategy: Assume a large induced subgraph F lacks the stated pure-or-x-sparse blockade. Apply the Rödl-initialized four-outcome theorem to F. The restricted, clique-or-stable-set, and complete-or-anticomplete blockade exits all contradict the ambient failure hypotheses after the source exponent comparisons, so the pure-or-x-sparse blockade outcome is forced.

items.title: Property (*) and leaf reducibility imply generalized niceness
items.strategy: Let x = epsilon^(5d). The previous lemma ensures that every epsilon^d-large induced subgraph has a pure or x-sparse polynomial blockade. Feed that local hypothesis into the published local-pure-or-x-sparse blockade theorem to obtain the first generalized-nice outcome. The other three generalized-nice outcomes are exactly the alternative branches already isolated by the Rödl-initialized theorem.

items.title: A four-tooth comb with a special vertex triggers property (*)
items.strategy: Write down a four-tooth comb together with one outside vertex complete to the blocks and anticomplete to the teeth, and verify directly that the configuration satisfies the trigger hypothesis in the definition of property (*).

items.title: The third outcome of property (*) gives a pure four-blockade
items.strategy: Start from a four-tooth comb with common block size w and compute that the pure-blockade branch of property (*) reduces each block to size w/16. The check keeps the distinction between a pure blockade and a complete or anticomplete blockade explicit.

items.title: The square-root rescaling in Lemma 4.4
items.strategy: Choose a sample value of l, set k = sqrt(l), and verify numerically that the source inequality |F|/l^(29c_4) >= |G|/k^d holds under the stated condition d >= 58c_4. This isolates the only non-obvious renormalization step in the proof of Lemma 4.4.

items.title: The epsilon^(5d) substitution in Claim 4.5.1 and Lemma 4.5
items.strategy: Pick sample d and epsilon, compute x = epsilon^(5d), and verify the four exponent comparisons that turn the bad alternatives in Claim 4.5.1 into the three forbidden outcomes of Lemma 4.5.
